clinicalPearls: Deficient production of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones produces the clinical features of hypopituitarism; most adult cases are acquired (Harrison 22e p.2992).

With pituitary compression or destruction, trophic hormone failure usually occurs sequentially: GH first, then FSH, LH, TSH, and ACTH last; in children growth retardation is often the presenting feature, in adults hypogonadism is the earliest symptom (Harrison 22e p.2992).

Clinical manifestations depend on which hormones are lost and the degree of deficiency: GH deficiency causes growth disorders in children and abnormal body composition in adults; gonadotropin deficiency causes menstrual disorders/infertility/loss of secondary sexual characteristics; TSH deficiency causes hypothyroidism; ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency; PRL deficiency causes failure of lactation (Harrison 22e p.2996).
Secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency causes hypocortisolism with relative preservation of mineralocorticoid production (unlike primary adrenal failure) (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency: acute intrapituitary hemorrhage/infarction presenting with severe headache, meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, ophthalmoplegia, and in severe cases cardiovascular collapse and loss of consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Lymphocytic hypophysitis occurs most often in postpartum women, presents with hyperprolactinemia and an MRI mass resembling an adenoma, and may be transient or permanent; it should be considered before unnecessary surgery in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Up to 20% of patients receiving CTLA-4 inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., ipilimumab) develop hypophysitis; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) can also cause it, sometimes with delayed presentation (Harrison 22e p.2993).
Patients on glucocorticoid replacement require careful dose escalation (stress dosing) during acute illness, dental procedures, trauma, and hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.2996).
harrison.pathophysiology: Impaired synthesis or secretion of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones (GH, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PRL), and sometimes posterior pituitary AVP. Causes are developmental/genetic (transcription factor mutations such as PROP1, PIT-1, TPIT, midline defects) or, more commonly in adults, acquired from compressive mass effect of tumors or from local pituitary/hypothalamic traumatic, autoimmune, inflammatory, infiltrative, or vascular damage. The same processes may impair hypothalamic hormone production with secondary pituitary failure. With progressive compression/destruction, hormone loss is typically sequential (GH > FSH > LH > TSH > ACTH) (Harrison 22e p.2992).
additionalDifferentials: Pituitary adenoma (mass on MRI may be indistinguishable from lymphocytic hypophysitis)
Craniopharyngioma, Rathke's cyst, meningioma, germinoma, glioma, ependymoma
Pituitary metastases (breast, lung, colon) and lymphoma/leukemia
Primary (target-organ) endocrine failure as opposed to central deficiency
infectionMimics: Fungal infection (histoplasmosis) and opportunistic fungal infection in AIDS
additionalInvestigations: Low target-organ hormone with low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone (e.g., low free thyroxine with low/inappropriately normal TSH = secondary hypothyroidism; low testosterone without elevated gonadotropins = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
GH reserve: insulin-induced hypoglycemia, arginine, glucagon, l-dopa, GHRH, or macimorelin; AGHD defined by peak GH response to hypoglycemia <3 ug/L
ACTH/cortisol reserve: most reliably assessed during insulin-induced hypoglycemia; CRH stimulation and cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) testing also used
Pituitary MRI or CT to identify mass, hemorrhage, stalk deviation, or empty sella; age-matched IGF-1 as an index of GH therapeutic response
redFlags: Pituitary apoplexy: an endocrine emergency that may cause severe hypoglycemia, hypotension/shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death; severe ophthalmoplegia or progressive visual loss indicates need for urgent surgical decompression
Secondary adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis: hypocortisolism that can precipitate life-threatening shock, especially during stress, illness, surgery, or trauma
Acute severe headache with meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, or loss of consciousness in a patient with known/suspected pituitary mass
harrison.prognosis: Hormone replacement is usually safe and effective at maintaining homeostasis when it mimics physiologic secretion. However, long-standing pituitary damage carries an increased mortality rate, primarily from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease; adult hypopituitarism is associated with an approximately threefold increase in cardiovascular mortality versus age- and sex-matched controls. Prior head/neck irradiation is an additional determinant of increased mortality, especially from cerebrovascular disease. Lymphocytic hypophysitis may resolve with recovery of pituitary function after glucocorticoid treatment depending on extent of damage; hypopituitarism is common after apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.2996).
pitfalls: Critical sequencing pitfall: in suspected combined deficiency, glucocorticoid replacement must be started BEFORE thyroid hormone, because giving thyroxine first can accelerate cortisol clearance and precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient with unrecognized secondary adrenal insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.3133).

Insulin-induced hypoglycemia testing must be performed cautiously in suspected adrenal insufficiency (enhanced susceptibility to hypoglycemia/hypotension) and is contraindicated in active coronary artery disease or known seizure disorders (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Lymphocytic hypophysitis may be radiologically indistinguishable from a pituitary adenoma and should be considered in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass before surgery is undertaken (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Radiation-induced and brain-injury-related hypopituitarism develops insidiously over 5-15 years (and in 25-40% after brain injury), so long-term periodic endocrine follow-up is required even after apparently successful treatment (Harrison 22e p.2993).
Empty sella patients usually have normal pituitary function, but hypopituitarism may develop insidiously (Harrison 22e p.2994).
